title: Batch norm on all layers causes oscillation
description: Directly applying batch normalization to all layers resulted in sample oscillation and model instability, requiring batchnorm to be omitted from the generator output and discriminator input layers.
canonical_description: applying batch normalization to all layers causes oscillation and instability

evidence.anchor: Directly applying batchnorm to all layers however, resulted in sample oscillation
evidence.quote: Directly applying batchnorm to all layers however, resulted in sample oscillation and model instability.

verdict.reasoning: Paper 2 provides partial empirical evidence relevant to one half of the gap: it finds that batch normalization should be avoided in the critic/discriminator of IPM-based GANs, especially under gradient-norm constraints, and notes that BN couples samples in the batch which creates problems. This aligns with the gap's observation that BN at the discriminator input (first layers) causes instability. However, Paper 2 does not examine the oscillation phenomenon itself, does not address the generator output layer (their generator still uses BN throughout), and its motivation is SSL accuracy rather than understanding/fixing the oscillation. Papers 1 and 3 are not_addressed — Paper 1 replaces BN entirely with Weight Normalization without studying the oscillation, and Paper 3 replaces BN with RBN for a different reason (noise-sample representation differences) while ignoring the oscillation problem altogether. Thus a meaningful piece of the gap remains open: the specific mechanism by which BN causes oscillation when applied to all layers, particularly the generator output layer, and any solution that would keep BN working across all layers.

paper.title: On the Effects of Batch and Weight Normalization in Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are highly effective unsupervised learning frameworks that can generate very sharp data, even for data such as images with complex, highly multimodal distributions. However GANs are known to be very hard to train, suffering from problems such as mode collapse and disturbing visual artifacts. Batch normalization (BN) techniques have been introduced to address the training. Though BN accelerates the training in the beginning, our experiments show that the use of BN can be unstable and negatively impact the quality of the trained model. The evaluation of BN and numerous other recent schemes for improving GAN training is hindered by the lack of an effective objective quality measure for GAN models. To address these issues, we first introduce a weight normalization (WN) approach for GAN training that significantly improves the stability, efficiency and the quality of the generated samples. To allow a methodical evaluation, we introduce squared Euclidean reconstruction error on a test set as a new objective measure, to assess training performance in terms of speed, stability, and quality of generated samples. Our experiments with a standard DCGAN architecture on commonly used datasets (CelebA, LSUN bedroom, and CIFAR-10) indicate that training using WN is generally superior to BN for GANs, achieving 10% lower mean squared loss for reconstruction and significantly better qualitative results than BN. We further demonstrate the stability of WN on a 21-layer ResNet trained with the CelebA data set. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/stormraiser/gan-weightnorm-resnet

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Weight Normalization (WN) as an alternative to Batch Normalization (BN) for training GANs, demonstrating that WN provides more stable training and better reconstruction quality than BN. The paper acknowledges the known issue that BN should not be applied to all layers (omitting it from the generator output and discriminator input layers), but does not attempt to solve or analyze the oscillation problem caused by applying BN to all layers. Instead, it proposes replacing BN entirely with WN.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the specific problem of why applying batch normalization to all layers causes oscillation and instability, nor does it propose any method to enable BN to be safely applied to all layers. The paper simply follows the existing practice of omitting BN from certain layers and proposes a different normalization technique (WN) as a replacement. The underlying question of what causes the oscillation when BN is applied to all layers, and how to fix it while keeping BN, remains completely open.
evidence_snippets: As per common practice, Batch Normalization is not applied to the first layer of the discriminator, nor to the last layers of both the discriminator and generator.

Our experiments show that BN generally accelerates training in early stages, and can increase the success rate of GAN training for certain datasets and network structures where a model without any normalization could often fail. In many cases though, BN can cause the stability and generalization power of the model to decrease drastically.

We found that batch-normalized models perform worse in reconstructing test samples and are less stable during training. In particular, both reconstruction errors and the visual quality can be deteriorated by BN. However, our formulation of weight normalization improves both reconstruction quality and training stability considerably.

paper.title: Semi-Supervised Learning with IPM-based GANs: an Empirical Study
paper.abstract: We present an empirical investigation of a recent class of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) using Integral Probability Metrics (IPM) and their performance for semi-supervised learning. IPM-based GANs like Wasserstein GAN, Fisher GAN and Sobolev GAN have desirable properties in terms of theoretical understanding, training stability, and a meaningful loss. In this work we investigate how the design of the critic (or discriminator) influences the performance in semi-supervised learning. We distill three key take-aways which are important for good SSL performance: (1) the K+1 formulation, (2) avoiding batch normalization in the critic and (3) avoiding gradient penalty constraints on the classification layer.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper empirically investigates normalization choices (batch norm, layer norm, no normalization) in the critic/discriminator of IPM-based GANs for semi-supervised learning. It finds that batch normalization should be avoided in the critic, especially when gradient-norm constraints are used, and that it also hurts performance for Fisher GAN. The paper recommends either layer normalization (with singleton statistics) or no normalization in the critic. This aligns with the gap's finding that BN on all layers is problematic, but the paper's focus is on SSL classification accuracy rather than studying the oscillation phenomenon itself.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not study, analyze, or explain the oscillation/instability phenomenon that occurs when batch normalization is applied to all layers. It does not investigate the specific mechanism by which BN causes oscillation, nor does it examine the "generator output and discriminator input layers" aspect mentioned in the gap. The paper's generator still uses BN (contradicting the gap's finding that BN should be omitted from the generator output), and the paper's recommendation to avoid BN in the critic is motivated by SSL performance degradation rather than oscillation/instability. The gap's specific problem — understanding and solving the oscillation caused by applying BN to all layers — remains open.
evidence_snippets: Unless noted otherwise this CNN will have no normalization (LN or BN) in the critic, but $g_\theta$ always includes BN.
Avoid batchnorm, definitely when constraining the gradient norm in objective, but it also hurts for Fisher GAN!
When the constraint involves a norm of the gradient, BN is problematic since it couples the different samples in the batch.

paper.title: GIU-GANs: Global Information Utilization for Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: In recent years, with the rapid development of artificial intelligence, image generation based on deep learning has dramatically advanced. Image generation based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) is a promising study. However, since convolutions are limited by spatial-agnostic and channel-specific, features extracted by traditional GANs based on convolution are constrained. Therefore, GANs are unable to capture any more details per image. On the other hand, straightforwardly stacking of convolutions causes too many parameters and layers in GANs, which will lead to a high risk of overfitting. To overcome the aforementioned limitations, in this paper, we propose a new GANs called Involution Generative Adversarial Networks (GIU-GANs). GIU-GANs leverages a brand new module called the Global Information Utilization (GIU) module, which integrates Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks (SENet) and involution to focus on global information by channel attention mechanism, leading to a higher quality of generated images. Meanwhile, Batch Normalization(BN) inevitably ignores the representation differences among noise sampled by the generator, and thus degrade the generated image quality. Thus we introduce Representative Batch Normalization(RBN) to the GANs architecture for this issue. The CIFAR-10 and CelebA datasets are employed to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model. A large number of experiments prove that our model achieves state-of-the-art competitive performance.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes GIU-GANs, which uses a GIU module (combining SE module and involution) for global information utilization, and replaces Batch Normalization with Representative Batch Normalization (RBN) in the generator to address the issue that BN ignores representation differences among noise samples. The discriminator does not use BN at all. However, the paper does not address the specific problem of oscillation caused by applying BN to all layers.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns oscillation and model instability caused by applying batch normalization to all layers (generator output and discriminator input). This paper does not investigate, discuss, or propose a solution to this oscillation problem. It addresses a different BN-related issue (BN ignoring representation differences among noise samples) and uses RBN in the generator while omitting BN from the discriminator entirely — but without framing this as a solution to oscillation. The specific problem of BN-on-all-layers causing oscillation remains entirely unaddressed.
evidence_snippets: Batch Normalization (BN) inevitably ignores the representation differences among noise sampled by the generator and thus degrades the generated image quality.
The discriminator does not use BN, and GIU-GANs select LeakReLU with the slope of the leak set to 0.1 and ReLU for the discriminator and generator, respectively.

However, $E(X)$ and $Var(X)$ of mini-batch use normalization to reduce the expression of partial random noise by the generator. Therefore, we replace the BN with RBN in part of the network layer of GANs.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: The gap is moderately tractable. Data availability is not a barrier (standard GAN benchmarks like CIFAR, CelebA, LSUN are freely available). Compute requirements are modest (single-GPU experiments suffice for studying the phenomenon on small-to-medium architectures). Methodological maturity is decent — one can systematically ablate BN placements, track BN running statistics vs. sample oscillation, measure gradient dynamics, and use established stability metrics (FID trends, gradient norms, oscillation amplitude across training steps). The scope is focused: it's not "understand all of GAN training" but specifically "why does BN at generator output / discriminator input cause oscillation, and can we fix it?" Evaluatability is clear — oscillation is measurable (variance of generator outputs across consecutive steps, mode collapse indicators, FID variance). The main feasibility challenges are: (1) mechanistic analysis of BN-induced coupling across mini-batches requires careful experimental design to separate causes from correlations, and (2) a solution keeping BN everywhere may require non-trivial architectural innovation (though known alternatives like ghost BN or instance normalization provide baselines). It does not require a fundamental breakthrough — it's an empirical investigation with clear hypotheses to test.
